title: Farms that climb the walls
text: Stack a greenhouse on itself a dozen times, control every photon and every drop of water, and you get vertical farming: lettuces grown under {{1}} light in windowless warehouses, metres from the customers who eat them. The {{2}} are real. Yields per square metre are enormous, pesticides are unnecessary in a sealed room, water use falls by up to ninety-five per cent, and crops can be grown in deserts or beside the Arctic Circle, {{3}} of climate. Yet the economics remain {{4}}: light is what the sun provides free, and paying for electricity to make it is the industry's central problem. Several high-profile ventures have gone {{5}} on precisely that point, and investors have grown cautious. The {{6}} is settling on pragmatic lines: leafy greens and herbs, which are light, perishable and valuable, work; wheat and rice, which need enormous energy to grow, do not. Critics call it a {{7}} that lets cities feel virtuous about salads while conventional farming, with all its problems, still feeds the world. Supporters answer that as LEDs grow more efficient and renewable electricity cheaper, the arithmetic {{8}} in the technology's favour, and that growing food beside the people who eat it may soon stop being a curiosity.

gaps.explanation: 'under artificial light' — produced by lamps; arduous = exhausting, aromatic = fragrant.
'the benefits are real' — the genuine advantages; bearer = a carrier, beacon = a signal light.
'grown in deserts, regardless of climate' — without being affected by it; 'regarding' means 'about' and takes no 'of'.
'the economics remain daunting' — intimidating; dawn = daybreak, darn = mend socks.
'ventures have gone bankrupt' — the fixed phrase for financial collapse; 'gone blank' describes a mind or screen.
'the industry is settling on pragmatic lines' — the sector as a whole; indulgence = a treat, induction = a formal introduction.
'a gimmick that lets cities feel virtuous' — a showy trick rather than real substance; gadget = a small device, gamble = a risky bet.
'the arithmetic tips in the technology's favour' — tilts the balance; tap = strike lightly, tug = pull sharply.
